# Apple Human Interface Guidelines

Use the relevant Apple guidance to make concrete design decisions. This package
contains a router, 13 family routes, 158 operational topic skills, and supporting
article-level references. It is
independent of Apple. The sources are a dated English HIG snapshot; check the
official source when a task depends on a newer release or a disputed detail.

## Route the task

1. Identify the target platform, device context, and user task from the request or
   project. Ask for the platform only when it materially affects the answer and
   cannot be inferred. Preserve the user's framework and product requirements.
2. Select the relevant family below and read that family's `SKILL.md`. Follow its
   link to the exact topic procedure under `.topics/` and read that `SKILL.md`.
   Apply its decision procedure, then consult its supporting article for facts
   and platform qualifications. Topic skills are explicitly read by installed
   file path; automatic nested discovery is not required.
   For platform support, product feasibility, or platform adaptation, first read each relevant
   platform's Getting started procedure, then the specific component or technology
   procedure. Check both the platform model and the surface's support limits.
3. Before finalizing the route, search the [complete topic index](references/topic-index.md)
   for the task's concepts as well as component or framework names. Its trigger
   descriptions connect everyday product requests to Apple's topic names; users
   need not name an Apple framework. Read the owning family and matching topic
   procedure before its supporting reference. Search relevant rows instead of
   loading the full corpus for a narrow question.
   For a screenshot-specific or animated example, also consult its
   [original visual explanation](references/media/index.md) when available.
4. Apply shared guidance and the target platform's documented differences. A
   missing platform subsection means no additional rule is stated; it does not
   prove support, nonapplicability, or identical behavior across platforms.
5. Compose families when the task crosses them: a component can also require
   accessibility, typography, localization, input, or system-experience guidance.
   Map the brief's material decisions to their owning topics. Read the owning
   procedure for each explicit concern, such as privacy or accessibility, as well
   as the affected components; a neighboring procedure's reminder is insufficient.
   Use [platform and task routes](references/platforms-and-tasks.md) when useful.
   In a review, map each supplied control to its candidate component procedure
   even when markup or behavior is missing. Use it to frame inspection questions;
   missing evidence neither proves a defect nor removes that control from scope.

All paths are relative to **this installed package**, not the shell's current
directory. No Python, network, sibling skill installation, or authoring cache is
required to read the guidance.

## Perform the requested work

Inspect the supplied brief, flow, code, specification or image before deciding
what is wrong or choosing a framework. Use the user's requested mode:

- **Design:** produce an implementable specification or interaction/state model
  from the topic's decision procedure, with concrete transitions and acceptance
  checks. Connect choices to the user's task and target platform.
- **Implement:** prefer the project's native system components when they supply
  the needed behavior. HIG explains experience requirements; verify API names,
  availability, and code against the appropriate SDK documentation. Make the
  authorized changes in the existing stack; a prose explanation alone does not
  complete an implementation request.
- **Review:** describe the observed problem, its effect, the relevant HIG rule,
  and a concrete correction. Separate source-backed findings from your own
  suggested improvements. Do not invent violations without inspecting evidence.
- **Adapt:** preserve the product task, data and useful state while applying the
  destination platform's interaction model. Patch the supplied artifact or give
  an explicit before/after contract when a design specification is requested.

Topic procedures are framework agnostic. Their worked examples and pseudocode
teach decisions, not a requirement to replace the project's technology. Load
related procedures only for a decision that actually depends on them.

Complete the topic's observable checks and report passed, failed and not executed
separately. Reading a file, citing Apple, or proposing a test does not establish
runtime behavior. Static code or screenshots cannot prove assistive-technology
order, native rendering, physical comfort, haptics, or SDK compilation.

Include official article/section links for material recommendations. Preserve
qualifications such as “consider,” “prefer,” and “avoid”; do not turn design
advice into invented universal requirements. Retain units and platform scope for
numerical specifications. If source passages conflict, describe the conflict
and the conservative application rather than silently changing the source.

## Source boundaries

This is comprehensive local guidance, not a verbatim Apple manual or an SDK API
reference. Original media explanations are supplementary to article references;
the source page remains useful for visual demonstrations. Source snapshots and
review status live in the repository's coverage report, outside ordinary skill
loading. Do not infer that a source has been independently reviewed just because
its local file exists.

Historical `navigation-bars` links now resolve to current Toolbars guidance;
`in-app-purchase` resolves to Apple In-App Purchase. The old Touch Bar and Messages
for Business HIG pages were unavailable at this snapshot. Do not fabricate their
current rules. Translations, archived pages, and complete linked SDK/WWDC libraries
are outside the source boundary.

# Apple HIG: Platform and task adaptation

Use this family to select and compose topic procedures. Infer the platform and
requested work from the supplied project; preserve its framework and constraints.

## Work through the decision

1. Identify the person’s primary task and the target platform before translating a screen. Read that platform’s procedure; use Principles to resolve hierarchy and Designing for games only for gameplay.
2. Compare navigation, window/scene model, primary input, attention duration and state restoration. Preserve the product task while changing the interaction appropriate to the destination platform.
3. For device changes such as opening an iPhone Duo or resizing an iPad window, specify what selection, editing state and route survive each transition.
4. Deliver a platform-decision matrix or an adaptation patch, with concrete acceptance scenarios for each materially different interaction.

name: apple-hig-designing-for-ios
description: Use when creating, reviewing, or adapting an iPhone experience for handheld touch, interrupted use, orientation changes, and system entrypoints.

# Make the iPhone task usable in the hand

Read [Designing for iOS](../../references/designing-for-ios.md). Inspect the current task, its entry and return points, supported orientations, input, and any supplied implementation. Distinguish a brief check from extended work. For a review, anchor problems to supplied screens/behavior; for design or adaptation, revise the requested artifact in its existing stack.

Choose what must remain immediately visible during the task. A brief check needs its result and primary action close together; extended editing can expose additional controls without crowding the initial screen. Put frequent touch actions within comfortable reach, generally toward the middle/lower display, while preserving system navigation and swipe-back behavior. Move secondary commands into a short discoverable path rather than shrinking every control to fit.

Trace interruption and resumption: preserve the selected item, draft, or playback context when another app takes focus. Specify portrait/landscape and enlarged-text rearrangements without inventing a new navigation hierarchy for each orientation. Use touch and onscreen keyboard as the baseline, then offer appropriate voice or accessory paths. Add location, biometric, payment, or motion features only when their benefit reduces task effort and access is appropriate.

For repeated out-of-app actions, choose a relevant system entrypoint and a precise destination: a quick action starts an action, search opens the found content, and a widget exposes a useful glance. Do not add every entrypoint to every app.

**Before → decision → after:** A parcel app opens a dense desktop-style table and requires opening three menus to find the latest delivery. A handheld glance needs delivery state first. The revised home screen shows the active parcel and “Show pickup code,” keeps history one step away, and returns a widget tap to that parcel rather than a generic home screen.

Deliver a revised screen/flow or implementation plus interruption, orientation, and text-size acceptance checks. Fail if the primary action becomes unreachable, Back conflicts with a custom gesture, or resuming loses work. Screenshot review cannot establish touch comfort or actual system integration; state pending device checks.

For detailed adaptation use [Layout](../../../apple-hig-foundations/.topics/apple-hig-layout/SKILL.md); for custom touch gestures use [Gestures](../../../apple-hig-inputs/.topics/apple-hig-gestures/SKILL.md); for a chosen glance use [Widgets](../../../apple-hig-system-experiences/.topics/apple-hig-widgets/SKILL.md).

# Designing for iOS Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-ios) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. An iPhone experience must work both during brief checks on the move and through extended games, browsing, or media sessions. People switch among apps frequently. ## Best practices - Design for a medium-sized, dense display viewed at roughly 1–2 feet, usually held in one or both hands. Accommodate portrait and landscape use. - Keep primary content and actions clear, with secondary operations reachable through a small number of interactions rather than many simultaneous controls. - Support touch gestures, onscreen keyboards, and voice; use motion sensors, nearby spatial interactions, or personal information only where they improve the task. - Put frequent touch controls within comfortable reach, commonly the middle or lower display. Preserve swipe-back navigation and list-row gestures. - Adapt to orientation, Dark Mode, and Dynamic Type without breaking context. - With permission, use platform data and services to reduce typing: location, biometric authentication, and payments are examples. - Integrate appropriate system entry points: widgets, Home Screen quick actions, Spotlight search, Shortcuts, and activity views. Their familiar behavior helps people act outside the main app. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-ios) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. #### Videos Apple’s linked design sessions provide demonstrations and additional implementation context; no video review is implied here.

# Guide a real proximity task through changing signal quality

Read [Nearby interactions](../../references/nearby-interactions.md). Inspect the intended nearby object/person, hardware capabilities, distance/direction use, activity context, and requested design/review/adaptation. Preserve the stack and verify device support before promising UWB. This source excludes macOS/tvOS/visionOS; Watch supplies distance only and participating watch apps must remain foregrounded.

Decide what proximity improves: finding an intended recipient, locating an object, or handing off audio is more useful than sensing for novelty. Combine distance, available direction, and task context before identifying a target; session-scoped identifiers are not permanent identities. Request appropriate permission while the app is in use and offer another way to complete the task.

Define feedback that becomes more precise as the person approaches and remains continuous while moving. Choose visual, sound, and haptic channels according to whether attention belongs on the display or surroundings. On iPhone, direction may disappear outside the sensor field while distance remains; do not replace a missing bearing with a confident invented arrow. Guide device holding implicitly where possible and explain degraded availability caused by obstacles/people when it affects the task.

**Before → decision → after:** A museum finder keeps pointing left after the direction signal disappears and blocks exhibit lookup when UWB is unavailable. Decision: uncertain bearing must not look authoritative, and finding information does not require sensing. After, the UI shows available distance with a clear direction-unavailable state and holding guidance, then restores directional feedback when valid; search/list selection remains a complete alternative.

Deliver a capability/signal-state feedback map and corrected artifact. Fail if distance-only data implies direction, loss of signal freezes misleading guidance, a Watch workflow assumes background participation, or the alternative cannot finish the task. Actual accuracy, sensor field, obstruction response, and haptic guidance require compatible hardware tests; mock data verifies state handling only.

Use [Privacy](../../../apple-hig-foundations/.topics/apple-hig-privacy/SKILL.md) for permissions and [Accessibility](../../../apple-hig-foundations/.topics/apple-hig-accessibility/SKILL.md) for feedback/input alternatives.

# Nearby interactions Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/nearby-interactions) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. NearbyInteraction uses Ultra Wideband on compatible devices, with permission while the app is used. Session-scoped random identifiers protect privacy. # Ask for precise access when its purpose is clear

Read [Privacy](../../references/privacy.md). Inspect the feature's actual data needs, transfers, storage, current permission flow, and supported platform. Establish design, review, or adaptation mode. Produce the requested copy/flow/data-handling changes in the existing stack; distinguish documented platform restrictions from additional application recommendations.

Map each requested category to a specific feature and minimum necessary scope. Remove collection without a concrete benefit; prefer on-device work where it avoids unnecessary transfer. Explain collection/use accurately and flag App Store disclosure updates needed when behavior changes. Respect private email and tracking choices rather than designing around them.

Ask when the person invokes the feature. Launch-time requests need an essential, obvious dependency. Write a short active purpose sentence explaining use and reason. If context is sufficient, omit a custom pre-alert; if explanation is essential, use one clear continuation to the real system alert without imitating Allow/Don't Allow. Keep the guide's special pre-alert restrictions distinct from ordinary onboarding. Tracking requires its system authorization before collection and must not be incentivized or manipulated.

Choose one-time location access for suitable individual tasks using the system location button on supported platforms; preserve permitted customization and all localized/accessibility-sized text. Protect secrets with established authentication/keychain mechanisms. For Mac, account for sandboxing/distribution and fast user switching. For visionOS, separate system rendering assistance from permission-gated Full Space ARKit data; gaze remains private, and imported phone-camera assumptions may need removal or content import.

**Before → decision → after:** A bird journal asks for contacts, microphone, and continuous location at launch although only “Attach current location” uses location. Decision: request only the specific action's needed access. After, journaling works immediately; the attachment action offers the supported location control, and its purpose explains adding the sighting's location.

Deliver a data-purpose/access matrix and corrected permission sequence/copy or implementation. Fail if collection precedes required consent, copy obscures the real use, or unrelated work is gated on optional access. Report code/flow evidence separately from actual authorization prompts and privacy-setting behavior; this procedure does not certify security or legal compliance.

Use [Sign in with Apple](../../../apple-hig-technologies/.topics/apple-hig-sign-in-with-apple/SKILL.md) for that authentication choice and [Augmented reality](../../../apple-hig-technologies/.topics/apple-hig-augmented-reality/SKILL.md) when room/camera access is essential.

# Privacy Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/privacy) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. Communicate collection and usage clearly and protect granted data. Keep App Store privacy disclosures accurate for new releases and updates; people rely on them before downloading. ## Best practices Collect only what the specific feature requires and make access as precise as possible. Respect Hide My Email, Mail Privacy Protection, and tracking choices. Prefer on-device processing, including Create ML/Neural Engine where useful, to avoid unnecessary server transfers. Use system encryption, key management, and established security protections, including CloudKit’s additional encrypted data types where available. ## Requesting permission Protected categories include personal/location/health/financial/contact information, user-created content, messages/calendar/music/gameplay/HomeKit data, media, Bluetooth/Wi-Fi/local network resources, camera/microphone, the advertising identifier, and permission-gated ARKit data in a visionOS Full Space. The system displays the app’s purpose string and stores choices/descriptions in privacy settings. Ask when the person invokes the relevant feature. Request at launch only when access is essential and obviously necessary, such as location for navigation or room information for a spatial game that needs walls. Write a short, specific, active, complete sentence in sentence case with a period, explaining both use and reason. Vague promises of a better experience and commands to enable access do not explain the need. ### Pre-alert screens, windows, or views Usually context explains the request. If extra explanation is essential, use one button clearly leading to the system alert, such as Continue/Next; do not label it Allow or mimic the actual consent choice. Do not add cancellation, close, or other actions except those needed for legal consent. These restrictions apply to pre-permission custom explanations, not ordinary unrelated onboarding screens. ### Tracking requests Show the AppTrackingTransparency alert before collecting tracking information, including if tracking begins at launch. Do not offer incentives, imitate a permission prompt, display an image of the alert, annotate behind it, or otherwise manipulate rushed choices. Such patterns can cause App Review rejection. A legally required consent view before/after the system alert is permitted by the source’s stated review guidance. ## Location button On iOS/iPadOS/watchOS, the system location button provides one-time access at the task’s moment of need. The first tap teaches and confirms its behavior through a system alert; later taps grant access without repeating that education. Authorization expires when app use ends. With no prior status it resembles Allow Once; an existing While Using status is unchanged. Use it for individual tasks such as attaching a location or finding a nearby item/store. Customize only the supplied title, filled/outline glyph, foreground/background colors, and corner radius. Keep all localized and accessibility-size text untruncated and maintain contrast/transparency limits. Persistent customization violations can prevent location access even though the button still triggers other app actions. ## Protecting data Prefer passkeys; if passwords remain, add two-factor verification. Use Face ID, Optic ID, or Touch ID to protect continued signed-in access where appropriate. Store secrets in the encrypted keychain, never plaintext files even with restrictive permissions. Prefer established authentication, Sign in with Apple, and Password AutoFill over invented schemes. ## Platform considerations No extra iOS/iPadOS/tvOS/watchOS rules are listed. ### macOS Sign externally distributed apps with a valid Developer ID. Use sandboxing to limit resource/data access; Mac App Store apps require it. Account for fast user switching rather than assuming the current person is the only signed-in account. ### visionOS System ARKit algorithms support lighting, mapping, persistence, segmentation, and related rendering in Shared Space without exposing raw data to apps. ARKit API access requires Full Space, and plane estimation, scene reconstruction, image anchoring, and hand tracking require permission. Gaze remains private: system hover feedback can respond before a tap without disclosing where someone looks. Compatibility back-camera input is blank; front-camera input represents spatial Personas with permission. Adapt imported phone/tablet camera-dependent features by removal or content import instead of assuming conventional camera capture. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/privacy) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. #### Videos Apple’s linked design sessions provide demonstrations and additional implementation context; no video review is implied here. ## Change log Source revision dates: June 21, 2023.

# Make the task accessible

Read [Accessibility guidance](../../references/accessibility.md) before applying platform values. This procedure turns that guidance into task-level changes; its artifact format and prioritization are application engineering advice, not additional Apple requirements.

## Establish what can be evaluated

Identify the supported platform, the person's task from entry to completion, and whether the request is design, review, or adaptation. Inspect the supplied screens, content, interaction description, semantics, or implementation. Record which evidence exists: a screenshot can establish visible labels and geometry, but cannot establish spoken names, focus order, alternative activation, or preference behavior. Continue using explicit assumptions when the platform or behavior is missing; ask only when the choice changes the requested result.

For a review, connect each finding to an observed barrier and its consequence for that task. Separate untested behavior needing verification from confirmed defects. For a design or adaptation, change the authorized artifact itself: a revised screen specification, interaction contract, or implementation. A general accessibility checklist alone is not the deliverable.

## Remove the barriers that the task contains

Trace the task without assuming sight, hearing, fine motor control, speech, or fast responses. Select the applicable branches:

- **Reading and visual distinctions:** Preserve content and available actions when text enlarges. Use the guide's platform-specific text defaults and minima; its resizing guidance is at least 200%, with 140% stated for watchOS. Reflow or expose another usable arrangement rather than clipping essential labels. Pair color distinctions with text, shape, or symbols. Evaluate actual foreground/background combinations in light and dark appearances; use a contrast calculator and preserve the guide's stated contrast-table scope instead of claiming that its values alone establish conformance. If the default scheme falls short, specify the Increase Contrast treatment.
- **Information carried by sound or imagery:** Identify what information would disappear when sound or sight is unavailable. Choose captions for synchronized audible events, subtitles for dialogue translation, audio description for visual events, or transcripts for a complete text account according to the content. Specify descriptions for meaningful interface/content imagery and omit redundant decoration. Pair essential sound feedback with a perceivable visual or appropriate haptic equivalent.
- **Manipulation and navigation:** Distinguish visible control size from its actual activation area and separation. Use the guide's platform default as the starting point; its smaller minimum is not a blanket recommendation for dense controls. Replace essential complex or repeated gestures with a labeled onscreen action. Make the complete task navigable and activatable with the supported keyboard and assistive input paths; speech must not be necessary. Preserve system accessibility shortcuts. For custom controls, specify names, roles, values, states, and task order rather than assuming their appearance supplies semantics.
- **Time, motion, and comprehension:** Give people time to read and act; prefer explicit dismissal when transient content requires attention. If motion is present, define a Reduce Motion version that retains state and meaning while reducing automatic movement, bounce, zoom, or depth changes. If media autoplays, provide playback control and consider a global preference; honor Dim Flashing Lights where applicable. Keep the task's navigation and wording consistent rather than adding instructional clutter.

Apply the relevant platform condition. For Assistive Access on iOS/iPadOS, focus on core tasks with one interaction per screen and the source's two confirmations for difficult-to-reverse actions in that mode. For visionOS, keep controls in comfortable view, avoid head-locked content and repeated large gestures, and accommodate hand/head Pointer Control and Zoom. These conditions do not apply automatically to every platform.

## Deliver and check the result

Return the revised artifact or evidence-based review, including the barrier, the concrete change, and its acceptance check. State which platform/preferences were considered and which claims remain unverified. Prioritize blockers to completing the task over cosmetic refinements.

Exercise each selected alternative along the same entry-to-completion path. Fail the check if essential content or actions disappear at the specified text scale, information remains available through only one sense, a required gesture has no equivalent, focus cannot reach/activate a necessary control, or a requested motion accommodation removes meaning. Measure contrast and activation geometry when the evidence permits; report missing measurements rather than inventing them. Use Accessibility Inspector and relevant VoiceOver, Switch Control, Full Keyboard Access, AssistiveTouch, or Pointer Control tests on supported Apple environments. Static inspection or a Linux run cannot establish those runtime results, Apple-device comfort, or App Store Accessibility Nutrition Label eligibility.

## Worked transformation

**Before:** An iPad astronomy log marks observation quality only with green/red dots, announces saving with a chime, and exposes Delete only by a two-finger gesture.

**Decision:** Logging must remain understandable without color or sound and operable without that gesture. Retain compact rows while making status and actions explicit.

**After:** Each row reads “Clear” or “Clouded” alongside its symbol; saving exposes a persistent “Saved” state; a labeled row action opens Delete. The screen specification includes expanded-text reflow, semantic row status, and keyboard/assistive activation acceptance checks. These are proposed changes until the actual implementation passes those checks; the specification does not claim VoiceOver was tested.

## Continue only where needed

For detailed spoken structure and rotor navigation, use [VoiceOver](../../../apple-hig-technologies/.topics/apple-hig-voiceover/SKILL.md). For text reflow/type choices use [Typography](../apple-hig-typography/SKILL.md); for a motion accommodation use [Motion](../apple-hig-motion/SKILL.md). If spatial comfort dominates the task, use [Spatial layout](../apple-hig-spatial-layout/SKILL.md). Keep the task's accessibility acceptance checks when handing off.

# Accessibility Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. Build an interface people can understand, perceive through different senses, and adapt to their preferred methods. Treat accessibility as a design input and audit with Accessibility Inspector. Evaluate actual support before describing Accessibility Nutrition Labels on the App Store. ## Vision Support text enlargement of at least 200%; the source gives 140% for watchOS. Dynamic Type or equivalent custom resizing must preserve usability. Follow platform defaults/minima when choosing custom styles, and enlarge thin-weight custom fonts further when needed. |Platform|Default text|Minimum text| |---|---:|---:| |iOS, iPadOS|17 pt|11 pt| |macOS|13 pt|10 pt| |tvOS|29 pt|23 pt| |visionOS|17 pt|12 pt| |watchOS|16 pt|12 pt| Measure contrast using established calculators such as WCAG or APCA. Apple’s Accessibility Inspector table uses these WCAG-AA guidance values: text up to 17 pt, all weights, 4.5:1; 18 pt at all weights, 3:1; bold text at any size, 3:1. Preserve the table’s stated scope rather than assuming it replaces a separate conformance evaluation. If default colors fall short, Increase Contrast must supply a higher-contrast scheme. Test both light and dark. Prefer semantic system colors that adapt to accessibility preferences. Pair color with shape, icons, or text; red/green and blue/orange distinctions can be difficult. Let people customize chart or character colors where useful. Give VoiceOver meaningful descriptions of interface and content. ## Hearing Make dialogue and important information available without sound. Captions describe audible information in synchrony with media, subtitles present dialogue in a chosen language, audio descriptions narrate otherwise visual events in audio pauses, and transcripts provide a complete text account of audible and visual information. Let people adjust text presentation. Pair sound feedback with matching haptics and visual direction cues, especially for offscreen game or spatial events. Music Haptics and audio graphs on iOS/iPadOS can offer tactile representations of music and data. ## Mobility Use comfortable controls and sufficient separation, not just adequate visible size. |Platform|Default control|Minimum control| |---|---:|---:| |iOS, iPadOS|44 × 44 pt|28 × 28 pt| |macOS|28 × 28 pt|20 × 20 pt| |tvOS|66 × 66 pt|56 × 56 pt| |visionOS|60 × 60 pt|28 × 28 pt| |watchOS|44 × 44 pt|28 × 28 pt| The source suggests around 12 pt padding for bezelled elements and 24 pt outside visible edges for elements without a bezel. Use simple gestures for repeated tasks and offer an onscreen alternative for essential gestures, such as a dismiss button alongside swipe-to-dismiss. Avoid requiring complex multiple-finger or multiple-hand actions. Label controls so Voice Control can target them. Siri/Shortcuts can expose repeated tasks through voice, Action buttons, Home Screen, and Control Center. Test VoiceOver, AssistiveTouch, Full Keyboard Access, Pointer Control, and Switch Control rather than assuming support. ## Speech Support complete keyboard navigation and Full Keyboard Access; preserve system accessibility shortcuts. Support Switch Control navigation and activation through hardware, controller, and sound inputs such as a click or pop, so speech is never a necessary input method. ## Cognitive Use familiar, simple, consistent navigation and gestures. Prefer explicit dismissal over timed disappearance, allowing time for processing and assistive navigation. Games can offer difficulty, reaction-time, success-criteria, and control-assistance accommodations. Give clear playback controls and consider a global autoplay preference. Respect Dim Flashing Lights during media playback. Honor Reduce Motion by reducing automatic and repeated movement, scaling, zooming, and peripheral effects. Reduce spring bounce; tie appropriate motion directly to gestures; avoid animated depth changes and blur transitions; replace spatial translations with fades. Fast or blinking motion can distract, cause dizziness, or trigger seizures. For Assistive Access on iOS/iPadOS, focus on core tasks, remove nonessential workflows, and split multistep tasks into one interaction per screen. The source requires two confirmations for actions that are difficult to reverse, such as deletion, in this mode. ## Platform considerations The source adds no separate rules for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, or watchOS beyond the guidance above. ### visionOS Support hand/head Pointer Control and Zoom. Keep controls inside a comfortable field of view; horizontal arrangements usually strain the neck less than tall ones. Avoid rapid shifts of attention among distant locations. Reduce peripheral animation speed and intensity, use gentle camera/video motion, and avoid making the surrounding world move without the person’s control. Do not lock content to the head, which can feel confining and interfere with Pointer Control. Minimize large or repeated gestures and consider the physical surroundings. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. #### Videos Apple’s linked design sessions provide demonstrations and additional implementation context; no video review is implied here. ## Change log Source revision dates: June 9, 2025, March 7, 2025, June 10, 2024, December 5, 2023, June 21, 2023.

# Revised nearby-item finding specification

## Scope and decisions

Replace the behavior described in "'`interface.md`: an iOS finder that always claims exact centimeter distance, points through walls without uncertainty, and breaks when direction disappears. The task is finding a selected physical item using an available accessory. Accessory presence alone does not establish ranging compatibility, identity, permission, accuracy, or direction support.

This is a framework-agnostic interaction contract, not SDK implementation. The following source links identify the official articles underlying the installed local guidance; no web retrieval was performed.

| Decision | Concrete behavior | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Gate precision by capability | Resolve selected accessory identity and phone/accessory compatibility before offering live guidance. Unknown support shows “Checking finding support…”; unsupported shows “Nearby guidance isn’t available for this item.” Never infer UWB from iPhone eligibility alone. | [Nearby interactions](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/nearby-interactions#Best-practices); product gating decision |
| Separate distance and direction | Show only fresh, usable measurements. Distance alone never generates an arrow. Reacquire direction without restarting the task. | [Nearby interactions: Device usage](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/nearby-interactions#Device-usage) |
| Communicate uncertainty | Use “About … away,” with precision limited by validated measurement quality. No universal centimeter claim, wall penetration claim, floor identification, or navigable route. Bearing means relative direction, not a safe path. | [Nearby interactions](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/nearby-interactions#Best-practices); conservative product interpretation |
| Ask at invocation | Request only access actually needed when the person taps “Find nearby.” Denial leaves item details and manual finding usable. | [Privacy: Requesting permission](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/privacy#Requesting-permission) |
| Keep an alternative through completion | “Find without nearby guidance” opens a manual checklist and explicit “I found it” completion. This does not promise physical recovery. | [Nearby interactions](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/nearby-interactions#Best-practices) |
| Preserve handheld context | Keep selected item, Back, and Stop available. Resume with new capability/permission/signal checks; never reuse a pre-interruption arrow. Support portrait and landscape. | [Designing for iOS](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-ios#Best-practices) |

## Entry, screen, and completion

Item details show the item’s existing name and identifying description/photo, if supplied. Selection identifies the intended item; a transient sensing identifier must not become its permanent identity. Primary action: **Find nearby**. Secondary action: **Find without nearby guidance**. Do not invent a last-known location, map, sound command, or pairing capability.

On Find nearby, check capability without starting protected sensing. If supported, request required permission if undetermined, then connect to the selected accessory. Example purpose copy, subject to actual integration review: “Use nearby interactions to estimate this item’s distance and direction while you find it.” Use the real platform authorization mechanism when available; do not simulate consent. Omit a custom pre-alert because this entry already explains the task. If no authorization mechanism or sensing provider exists, use the unsupported state.

Finding screen, in order: item name; persistent state text; available distance; available relative direction and matching text; short contextual guidance; actions. Keep **Stop finding** and **Find without nearby guidance** reachable, generally in the middle/lower display. Back stops the session and returns to the same item. **I found it** ends sensing and shows “Finding complete” until explicitly dismissed; proximity alone never marks success.

## Capability and signal-state feedback map

These states are mutually exclusive display modes; permission and capability failures take precedence over signal data.

| State / trigger | Display and actions | Next transition |
|---|---|---|
| Checking / unknown support | “Checking finding support…”; no numeric estimate or arrow; manual option and Stop remain available | Capability result → unsupported, permission, or connecting |
| Unsupported | “Nearby guidance isn’t available for this item.” Manual option; Retry support check; item details | Retry rechecks rather than assuming success |
| Permission undetermined | Real authorization request after invocation; no ranging before grant | Grant → connecting; denial/restriction → access unavailable |
| Access unavailable | “Nearby guidance is unavailable with current access.” Manual option; show “Review access” only if a verified settings route exists | Explicit Retry rechecks access; never repeatedly prompt on its own |
| Connecting / no usable sample yet | “Connecting to [item]…”; no estimate or arrow | Valid sample → corresponding live state; failure → disconnected |
| Distance and direction usable | “About 2.5 m away” and arrow with “To your right,” for example; “Direction points toward the item, not a route around obstacles.” | Re-evaluate on every sample or validity expiry |
| Distance only | “About 2.5 m away · Direction unavailable.” Remove arrow immediately. “Try holding iPhone upright and gently turning toward the item.” A simple upright-phone illustration may supplement this text. | Direction returns → full guidance; distance fails → uncertain |
| Direction only | Relative arrow/text only if independently valid; “Distance unavailable.” Do not imply proximity | Distance returns → full guidance; bearing fails → uncertain |
| Uncertain / degraded | “Can’t estimate reliably right now.” No live number or arrow. “People or large objects between you and the item can affect guidance. Try a clearer position.” | Usable data → live state; explicit connection loss → disconnected |
| Disconnected / accessory lost | “Connection lost. Move closer if possible, then try again.” No frozen live measurements. Retry and manual option | Retry → capability/access checks, then connecting |
| Interrupted / app inactive | Stop presenting live data and release active sensing as integration permits; retain selected item and manual checklist | Return → “Resume finding” → fresh checks; no automatic permission prompt |
| Found / stopped | End session; clear samples and session identifiers | Done returns to selected item |

Do not treat an obstacle as detected: the obstruction copy describes a possible cause. Do not tell the person to walk through a wall or infer an unobstructed path from bearing. Holding guidance is optional assistance, never a required gesture or a substitute for the manual path.

### Provider contract and rendering pseudocode

The integration must supply independently qualified values, connection state, timestamps, and verified identity binding. If it cannot qualify freshness/quality, treat that value as unavailable. Session identifiers are temporary and must be bound to the selected accessory using a verified integration mechanism before guidance begins.

```text
on FindNearby:
    preserve selectedItem
    check phone + accessory + provider compatibility
    if unknown or unsupported: render corresponding state; return
    request only required access if undetermined
    if not granted: render accessUnavailable; return
    start new session bound to selectedItem

on sample or validity-expiry timer:
    reject samples from old sessions or a different item
    d = finite nonnegative distance AND provider-qualified quality AND fresh
    b = valid relative bearing AND provider-qualified quality AND fresh
    if not active, authorized, compatible, connected, identityBound:
        clear all live guidance; render applicable non-live state
    else:
        render full / distanceOnly / directionOnly / uncertain from (d, b)

on Stop, Back, Found, access revocation, or session replacement:
    end active session; invalidate samples and scheduled feedback
```

Freshness expiry, quality thresholds, and display rounding are integration parameters requiring hardware validation, not HIG numbers. Until a provider supplies validated limits, suppress live guidance. Proposed formatting policy: use localized units, “About,” and no more precision than the validated uncertainty supports; become more detailed only when quality supports it as the person approaches. Distance is straight-line separation, not walking distance. Do not translate decreasing distance into “warmer” unless the change exceeds validated noise. Update continuously from usable samples; remove expired guidance even if no further sample arrives.

## Alternative, privacy, and sensory access

Manual finding opens the same item’s identifying details plus a checklist: “Check where you last used it,” “Check pockets, bags, and nearby surfaces,” and an optional user-entered search note. Provide **I found it**, **Keep looking**, and **Back to item**. This path works with denied permission, unsupported hardware, a disconnected accessory, and no sensing provider. Notes survive interruption; do not claim a recorded location exists. An optional **Play sound** may be added only after accessory support, command delivery, and permissions are established; command failure must retain the checklist. It is outside the baseline contract.

Data-purpose/access matrix:

| Data | Purpose / access | Retention decision |
|---|---|---|
| Selected item identity/details | Identify the intended target; existing app data | Preserve under existing item-data policy |
| Relative distance/direction, quality, timestamps | In-use guidance, after required consent | Process locally; keep only current session samples; no server transfer or history in this proposal |
| Session identifier | Bind active sensing to selected item | Clear at session end; never use as persistent identity |
| Manual checklist/note | Continue a user-directed search; no sensor access | Keep locally until user clears it or item is removed |

No GPS, camera, microphone, contacts, or background tracking is assumed necessary. Verify any transport-specific access before implementation and update actual privacy disclosures if collection changes. These minimization choices follow [Privacy: Best practices](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/privacy#Best-practices).

All essential state and direction information has text equivalents; color and an arrow alone are insufficient. Use labeled actions with iOS default activation areas of at least 44 × 44 pt as the design target. Permit at least 200% text enlargement with reflow, keeping all actions available by scrolling. Controls need meaningful names, roles, enabled states, and current values; dynamic guidance must remain available to assistive technology without moving focus on every sample.
